name: GET operation retries on 503
description: Verifies that GET operations automatically retry on 503 Service Unavailable with exponential backoff. The success body uses the legacy single-key envelope, which every runner unwraps to a bare array before the wire; project_count 0 pins that unwrap parity (an enveloped body leaks through as 1 pseudo-item).

name: GET operation retries on 429 with Retry-After
description: Verifies that 429 responses respect the Retry-After header

name: POST operation does NOT retry (not idempotent)
description: Verifies that POST operations do NOT retry since they are not idempotent

name: Non-retryable error not retried
description: Verifies that 404 errors are not retried

name: Retry-After HTTP-date format respected
description: Verifies that Retry-After header with HTTP-date format is parsed and the SDK retries (2A.5). Uses a past date; the SDK should parse the date format, compute a non-positive delay, fall back to standard backoff, and still retry.

name: POST with 429 is not retried
description: Verifies that POST operations receiving 429 are NOT retried since POST is not idempotent (2B.4)

name: 403 Forbidden is not retried
description: Verifies that 403 Forbidden errors are not retried since they lack @retryable (2B.5)

name: GET 500 is not retried
description: 500 is absent from every operation's declared retryOn [429, 503]; the declared set gates status retries in all six SDKs, so a 500 must surface after exactly one attempt. Pins the #485 Ruby fix: its error taxonomy calls 500 retryable, but the taxonomy must not widen the declared set for governed traffic.

name: max_retries 0 sends exactly one request on a governed operation
description:
`max_retries = 0` is a legal spelling of "no retries — exactly one attempt", not a request to send nothing (SPEC §2 validation step 4). Until #718 the spec said `⊥` here and hand-written Go agreed by panicking at construction, while the other four numeric SDKs already accepted and floored the value — a contradiction with SPEC §14's own attempt-budget table, which had blessed "a zero cap" as yielding exactly one attempt all along.

`GetProject` is governed: it carries a `retry.max` of 3 in behavior-model.json, and 503 is in its declared `retry_on` set, so every retrying SDK would otherwise make three attempts here. In Go this case is red twice over against un-fixed code — first because client construction panicked, and then, once it did not, because the typed operation ran on the generated client's DefaultRetryConfig and made three requests: `initGeneratedClient` never passed the caller's cap at all.

A single 503 is queued deliberately: an SDK that retried would send a second request, fall off the end of the queue and get the mock's end-of-queue 500, so `requestCount: 1` cannot pass vacuously — it fails on the count either way.

**Strength is not uniform across the six runners, and this fixture does not pretend otherwise.** Go, Python, Ruby and Swift consult the budget BEFORE the first request (pre-check loops), so a zero cap is a real regression guard there. Kotlin and TypeScript consult it after, so a budget of 0 and of 1 are observably identical in those two — the same asymmetry #713 hit. TypeScript additionally has no numeric cap at all: the override maps to `enableRetry: false`, which is its spelling of the same contract (SPEC §2 validation step 4), as it does in Swift.

name: max_retries 0 sends exactly one request on ungoverned download traffic
description:
The companion to the governed case, on the one conformance-reachable path with NO operation entry in behavior-model.json. Every modelled operation in behavior-model.json carries a retry block, so "ungoverned" cannot mean an operation that lacks one — it means traffic with no operation ID at all, and `DownloadURL` is the reachable example (SPEC §14 hop-1 retry). With no per-operation ceiling to clamp it, the client cap is the entire budget, which is what makes this the case where a missing floor is unmasked rather than hidden behind a `min(cap, op_max)`.

503 is in the hop-1 retry set, so a retrying SDK sends a second request here. In hand-written Go the download loop is a separate pre-check loop from the GET one and needed its own floor: against un-fixed code a zero cap skipped it entirely and returned a usage error having sent nothing.

A single 503 is queued deliberately: an SDK that retried would send a second request, fall off the end of the queue and get the mock's end-of-queue 500, so `requestCount: 1` cannot pass vacuously — it fails on the count either way.

**Strength is not uniform across the six runners, and this fixture does not pretend otherwise.** Go, Python, Ruby and Swift consult the budget BEFORE the first request (pre-check loops), so a zero cap is a real regression guard there. Kotlin and TypeScript consult it after, so a budget of 0 and of 1 are observably identical in those two — the same asymmetry #713 hit. TypeScript additionally has no numeric cap at all: the override maps to `enableRetry: false`, which is its spelling of the same contract (SPEC §2 validation step 4), as it does in Swift.
